The project was implemented under Phase II of the Energizing Education Programme (EEP), funded by the World Bank and implemented by the Rural Electrification Agency (REA). The programme covers seven Nigerian universities and two teaching hospitals across the country’s six geopolitical zones.
Speaking at the commissioning, on Wednesday, Tegbe said the federal government’s approach to improving electricity supply combines stronger grid infrastructure with renewable and distributed energy systems adapted to the needs of different communities and institutions.
“Universities, healthcare facilities, and productive centres require solutions that respond to their actual needs,” he said.
He said the administration of President Bola Ahmed Tinubu is working to address electricity constraints that affect economic activity, while also supporting access to education for young Nigerians.
The managing director of the REA, Dr Abba Aliyu, said the facility comprises a 3MW solar hybrid power plant, 2.2MWh of battery energy storage, rehabilitated distribution infrastructure, streetlights and a renewable energy training centre.
He said the project is intended to support research, agricultural innovation, extended learning hours and entrepreneurship at the university.
Aliyu said the EEP has delivered energy infrastructure in 22 federal universities and three affiliated teaching hospitals, with more than 100MW of installed capacity. He said the programme has reached more than 600,000 students and 50,000 academic and non-academic staff.
He added that, under EEP Phase II, 140 female students in science, technology, engineering and mathematics have received practical renewable energy training.
Aliyu also said the completed Nigeria Electrification Project delivered 198 mini-grids and supported the deployment of about 1.4 million solar home systems across Nigeria.
He said the $750 million World Bank-supported Distributed Access through Renewable Energy Scale-up programme, DARES, is targeting electricity access for 17.5 million Nigerians and includes plans for about 1,350 mini-grids.
The Abia State governor, Dr Alex Otti, said the project would benefit lecturers, students and persons involved in scientific research.
Otti, who was represented by the Commissioner for Power, Hon. Ikechukwu Monday, thanked the federal government for its electrification efforts in Abia State and other parts of the country.
The head of the Nigeria Electrification Project, Femi Akinyelure, said Nigeria is expanding its energy-access capacity and aims to develop local capacity in renewable energy technology.
The vice-chancellor of the university, Prof. Ursula Ngozi Akanwa, said reliable electricity is necessary for the institution’s work in agricultural development, scientific research, innovation and practical responses to national challenges.
She said laboratories, workshops, research facilities and practical training programmes require a stable power supply to function.
Prof. Akanwa said the project addresses an infrastructure need and will support the university’s academic and research activities.
She pledged that the university would manage the facility properly and use electricity responsibly.
